content: Citrate, butylated hydroxyanisole, candelilla wax, cellulose acetate, confectioner’s sugar (which contains corn starch), FD&C Yellow 6, glyceryl monostearate, hypromellose, hypromellose phthalate, lactose, methacrylic acid copolymer type B, polyethylene glycols (PEG 400, PEG 8000), polyethylene oxides, polysorbate 80, propylene glycol, silicon dioxide, sodium chloride, sodium lauryl sulfate, synthetic black iron oxide, red iron oxide, talc, titanium dioxide, and triacetin are all components or excipients used in the formulation of the drug. Pharmacodynamics: Lovastatin and some of its metabolites exhibit pharmacological activity in humans. The liver serves as the primary site of action, being the main location for cholesterol synthesis and low-density lipoprotein (LDL) clearance. The role of LDL cholesterol (LDL-C) in the development of atherosclerosis has been extensively documented through clinical, pathological, and animal studies. Epidemiological and clinical research has demonstrated that elevated LDL-C levels and reduced high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C) levels are both associated with an increased risk of coronary heart disease (CHD). However, the risk of CHD is continuous and graded across the spectrum of cholesterol levels, and coronary events can occur even in individuals with lower total cholesterol (Total-C) and LDL-C levels. Immediate-release lovastatin tablets have been shown to effectively reduce elevated LDL-C concentrations. LDL is derived from very low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) and is primarily metabolized by high-affinity LDL receptors. The LDL-lowering effect of lovastatin may involve both a reduction in VLDL-C concentrations and an upregulation of LDL receptors, leading to decreased production and/or increased catabolism of LDL-C. The independent effects of raising HDL or lowering triglycerides (TG) on the risk of coronary and cardiovascular morbidity and mortality have not been definitively established. Additionally, the effects of lovastatin on lipoprotein(a), fibrinogen, and other independent biochemical risk markers for CHD remain unknown. Pharmacokinetics: Absorption: The absorption of lovastatin from an extended-release tablet is slower and more prolonged compared to the immediate-release formulation. Pharmacokinetic studies have measured systemic concentrations of lovastatin (pro-drug), lovastatin acid (active drug), and total and active inhibitors of HMG-CoA reductase. In hypercholesterolemic subjects at steady state after 28 days of treatment, the pharmacokinetic parameters of lovastatin 40 mg extended-release were compared to those of lovastatin 40 mg immediate-release. The extended-release formulation exhibited a prolonged absorptive phase, resulting in a longer time to maximum concentration (Tmax) and lower maximum concentration (Cmax) for both lovastatin and its major metabolite, lovastatin acid, compared to the immediate-release formulation. Bioavailability: The bioavailability of lovastatin (pro-drug), as measured by the area under the curve (AUC0-24hr), was greater for the extended-release formulation compared to the immediate-release formulation when assessed using a chemical assay. However, the bioavailability of total and active inhibitors of HMG-CoA reductase was equivalent between the two formulations when measured using an enzymatic assay. Lovastatin demonstrates dose linearity for doses ranging from 10 mg to 60 mg per day. Food intake decreases the bioavailability of lovastatin, with bioavailability being highest under fasting conditions and progressively lower when administered before bedtime, with dinner, or with a high-fat breakfast. Excretion: Following an oral dose of radiolabeled lovastatin in humans, approximately 10% of the dose is excreted in urine, while 83% is excreted in feces. The fecal excretion represents both absorbed drug equivalents excreted in bile and any unabsorbed drug. Timing of Administration: In a multicenter, randomized, parallel-group study, patients were administered 40 mg of lovastatin at three different times: before breakfast, after dinner, and at bedtime. While there was no statistically significant difference in the extent of lipid changes between the groups, numerically greater reductions in LDL-C and TG and an increase in HDL-C were observed when lovastatin was administered at bedtime.
